To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
FlhA (a) is a flagellar protein, (b) belongs to a family of putative signalling receptors and (c) is required in trans to form some, but not other, motility‐related products.

the B. subtils flhA gene encodes an integral membrane protein that is a member of a new family of putative receptors, and that flhA plays a role in the biosynthesis of some, but not other, B. subtlis motility‐associated operons.

the B. subtils flhA gene encodes a 67.7‐kDa protein that is a strong homologue of a family of proteins that are putative signal‐receptors and that is required in trans to form products from some flagellar operons.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structure and function of a flagellar gene, flhA, and its product FlhA, in B. subtili.
the identification, isolation and characterization of genes involved in the biosynthesis of motility in bacteria.
the identification and characterization of the genes and proteins that are involved in the assembly of the flagellin‐containing flagellum.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the FlhA protein is an integral membrane protein that functions in signal transduction during the biosynthesis and/or function of the flagellated cell.
FlhA, a putative integral membrane protein, is a flagellar protein required in trans for expression of some motility‐related genes.
the flhA gene encodes a signal transducing protein which is involved with the regulation of flagellar gene transcription.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
FlhA has a function that is similar to the CheA and CheW proteins of Escherichia coli.
we have identified the first flagellar protein from a Gram‐negative bacterium that is homologous to a signal‐transduceiving receptor.

FlhA, like the FlgS protein of Escherichia coli, is a member of a family of signal‐receptor proteins, and that FlhS and FlhA together comprise a two‐component regulatory system that is required for the biosynthesis of some flagellar products in B. subtils.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the flagellar protein FlhA is related to a newly identified group of signal‐transduction proteins that are involved in diverse processes.
FlhA, the product of the flhA gene, is the first member in a family of putative transmembrane receptors to be identified from a Gram‐Positive bacteria.
the FlhA protein of B. subtils is a signal transducing protein that is involved with flagellum formation.
